title: Decision Trees
description: Recursive partitioning for classification and regression: impurity measures, the CART algorithm, pruning and the limits of single trees.
overview: A decision tree asks a sequence of simple questions about the features, each splitting the data in two, until the answer is clear enough to predict. The result is a flowchart that a person can read, that handles numeric and categorical features without scaling, and that captures interactions between features automatically.

A single tree is weak on its own: it overfits easily, and small changes in the data give a very different tree. But trees are the building block of random forests and gradient boosting, which are among the strongest methods for tabular data. This chapter builds one tree, and the next chapter combines many.
objectives: Describe how a tree partitions the feature space and makes predictions.
Compute entropy, Gini impurity and information gain for a split.
Run the greedy CART procedure by hand for classification and regression.
Control overfitting with stopping rules and cost-complexity pruning.
State the strengths and weaknesses of single trees.

sections.title: How a decision tree predicts
body: A decision tree works like the game of twenty questions. To decide whether a bank should approve a loan, ask "Is income above 40,000?" If no, ask "Does the applicant have a past default?" and answer from that. If yes, ask a different question, such as "Is the debt ratio below 0.3?" Each answer narrows the group of applicants, and when a group is nearly all approved or nearly all rejected, you stop and answer. Training a tree means choosing which questions to ask, and in what order, from the data.

More precisely, a **decision tree** is a binary tree. Each internal node tests one feature against a threshold (x_j ≤ t for numeric features, or membership in a set for categorical ones) and sends the example left or right. Each **leaf** holds a prediction: the majority class of the training examples that reach it, or their mean for regression. Equivalently, the tree cuts the feature space into axis-aligned boxes and predicts a constant in each box.

body: Prediction is fast: it follows one path of length at most the depth, so it needs O(depth) comparisons. A tree can represent any Boolean function (with enough nodes), and it can represent interactions that a linear model needs explicit features for. For example, the rule 'x₁ > 0 XOR x₂ > 0' needs two levels.

sections.title: Impurity and information gain
body: Training chooses the splits. A good split makes the two resulting groups **purer**, with each group dominated by one class. A group of 10 examples that are all positive is perfectly pure: we can answer without doubt. A group split 5 positive and 5 negative is as impure as possible: guessing is a coin flip. We need a number that is 0 for the first group and largest for the second. For a node whose examples have class proportions p₁, …, p_K, three impurity measures are in use:

eqs: 0 for a pure node, log₂ K when all classes are equally likely
the chance that two random draws from the node have different classes
too coarse to guide the search

body: For two classes, here are the values at a few proportions of the positive class: p = 0 or 1 gives entropy 0 and Gini 0 (pure); p = 0.1 gives entropy 0.47 and Gini 0.18; p = 0.3 gives 0.88 and 0.42; p = 0.5 gives 1 and 0.5 (the most mixed). Entropy can be read as the average number of yes/no questions you would still need to ask to learn an example's class.
Entropy and Gini are smooth, strictly concave functions of the proportions, so they reward partial progress that the error rate ignores. They give nearly identical trees in practice.
For a split that sends N_L of the N examples left and N_R right, the **information gain** is the drop in impurity, with each child weighted by its size:

example.title: Comparing two splits
example.problem: A node has 6 positive and 4 negative examples. Split A sends (4+, 1−) left and (2+, 3−) right. Split B sends (4+, 0−) left and (2+, 4−) right. Compute the entropy gain and the Gini gain for each.
solution: Split B. Left is pure (H = 0, G = 0). Right (1/3, 2/3): H = 0.918, G = 0.444. Weights 4/10 and 6/10:
Both measures prefer split B, which produces a pure child.

body.note: Information gain with entropy is the mutual information between the split and the class label (see Information Theory in the Mathematics book). Using it, a tree is built to learn as much about the label per question as possible.

sections.title: Growing a tree: CART
body: The CART (classification and regression trees) algorithm grows a tree greedily from the root.

list: At a node, consider every feature and every candidate threshold. For a numeric feature, sort the values and test the midpoints between consecutive distinct values (at most m − 1 candidates). For a categorical feature, test subsets of categories.
Choose the split with the largest impurity decrease.
Recurse on the two children until a stopping rule applies: the node is pure, it has fewer than a minimum number of examples, the depth limit is reached, or the best gain is below a threshold.

body: After sorting a feature once, the impurity of every threshold can be updated incrementally in a single pass, so one node costs O(n m log m) over n features and m examples. Growing a balanced tree costs O(n m log² m) in all.

body.key: The procedure is greedy: each split is the best one now, with no look-ahead. Finding the globally smallest tree is NP-hard, and greedy search works well enough in practice.

body: For a numeric target, the leaf prediction is the mean of its examples, and the impurity is the sum of squared errors around that mean. A split is chosen to minimize SSE_left + SSE_right.

example.title: A regression split
example.problem: Data (x, y): (1, 1.0), (2, 1.2), (3, 0.9), (4, 5.0), (5, 5.2), (6, 4.9). Compare the SSE with no split and with the split x ≤ 3.5.
solution: The split reduces the error from 24.09 to 0.093, and the two leaves predict 1.03 and 5.03: a step function that matches the data.

list: A categorical feature with q levels has 2^{q−1} − 1 binary partitions. For two-class or regression problems, sort the levels by mean response and test only the q − 1 cuts along that order, which is optimal.
Many implementations send missing values down the more common branch, or learn a default direction for them at each split (surrogate splits).
Trees are invariant to monotone transformations of a feature: taking the logarithm changes nothing. No scaling is needed.

sections.title: Overfitting and pruning
body: A fully grown tree continues until every leaf is pure, which fits the training set perfectly, including its noise: a tree with one leaf per example has zero training error and poor generalization. Two ways to limit complexity:

list: **Pre-pruning** (early stopping): limit the depth, require a minimum number of examples in a leaf or for a split, or require a minimum gain. Simple, but a split with little gain can lead to an excellent split below it.
**Post-pruning**: grow a large tree, then remove branches that do not pay for themselves.

body: The idea of cost-complexity pruning is to charge a fee for every leaf. A branch with several leaves is kept only if the training error it removes is worth the fees. Raising the fee prunes more of the tree. In **cost-complexity pruning**, for a penalty α ≥ 0 define

where R(T) is the training error of the tree T and |T| is its number of leaves. For each α there is a unique smallest subtree minimizing R_α. Collapsing an internal node t into a leaf raises the error from R(T_t) to R(t) and removes |T_t| − 1 leaves, so it pays off once
Repeatedly collapse the 'weakest link' with the smallest such value to obtain a nested sequence of trees, and pick α (and so the tree) by cross-validation.

example.title: When to prune a branch
example.problem: A node t as a single leaf has error 0.08. Its subtree T_t has 3 leaves and error 0.05. For which α does pruning the subtree reduce the cost-complexity objective?
example.solution: Collapsing saves 3 − 1 = 2 leaves and costs an extra error of 0.08 − 0.05 = 0.03. It is worthwhile when α · 2 ≥ 0.03, i.e. α ≥ 0.015.

check.q: In cost-complexity pruning, a larger α produces
wrong: a deeper tree
zero training error
the same tree

sections.title: Strengths and weaknesses

head: Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: High variance: a small change in the data can change the root split and everything below
No feature scaling; handles mixed types
Piecewise-constant predictions; poor at smooth or additive relationships
Axis-aligned splits waste depth on diagonal boundaries
Greedy search can miss better trees
Robust to outliers in the inputs
Biased toward features with many possible splits
table.caption: A single decision tree.

body: The importance of a feature is the total impurity decrease (weighted by the fraction of examples reaching each node) over all the splits that use it. It ranks features cheaply, but it favors features with many distinct values and is unreliable when features are correlated. Permutation importance, which measures how much held-out accuracy drops when a feature is shuffled, is more trustworthy.

body.key: Trees have low bias when deep and high variance. Averaging many different trees reduces variance without raising bias. That observation leads directly to bagging, random forests and boosting.

check.q: The main weakness of a single deep tree is
wrong: high bias
inability to handle categorical data
sensitivity to feature scale

quiz.q: A trained tree has depth 5 and 40 leaves. At most how many feature tests are needed to classify one new example?
wrong: The number of features
quiz.why: Prediction follows a single root-to-leaf path and makes one test per level, so the cost is bounded by the depth, not the number of leaves.

quiz.q: Labels follow (x₁ > 0) XOR (x₂ > 0). Why can a depth-2 tree classify the data perfectly when one split cannot?
quiz.a: After the first split, each side can use a different test on the other feature
wrong: A depth-2 tree can draw a diagonal boundary through the origin by combining two splits
A leaf can store the XOR rule directly as its prediction
Two splits are averaged, which cancels the errors of each
quiz.why: Each split is axis-aligned, but the second-level tests are conditional on the first answer. That is how a tree captures an interaction.

quiz.q: Every value of a positive feature is replaced by its logarithm before training. What happens to the tree CART builds?
quiz.a: The same partition of the training examples results, with thresholds moved
wrong: The tree gets deeper, since the feature spacing changes
The splits change, because the feature's scale changes the impurity of every candidate split
The tree is invalid until the feature is standardized
quiz.why: A split only depends on the ordering of the feature values. A monotone transformation keeps the ordering, so the same examples go left and right.

quiz.q: A node holds four classes in equal proportions. Its Gini impurity is
quiz.why: G = 1 − 4(0.25)² = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. The value 0.25 is the proportion of each class, not the impurity.

quiz.q: A node is 25% positive and 75% negative. Its entropy is closest to
wrong: 0.375 bits
0.25 bits
0.5 bits
quiz.why: H = −0.25 log₂ 0.25 − 0.75 log₂ 0.75 = 0.5 + 0.311 = 0.811. The value 0.375 is the Gini impurity of the same node.

quiz.q: A parent node has 8 examples with Gini 0.375. A split sends 3 examples to a pure left child and 5 to a right child with Gini 0.48. What is the Gini gain?
quiz.why: The weighted child impurity is (5/8)(0.48) = 0.3, so the gain is 0.375 − 0.3 = 0.075. Averaging the children without weights would give 0.135.

quiz.q: Why do trees choose splits with entropy or Gini rather than the misclassification rate?
quiz.a: A split can leave the error rate unchanged while still making the children purer
wrong: The error rate cannot be computed for a child node that holds too few examples
Entropy and Gini give a different tree for every dataset
The error rate is not bounded between 0 and 1
quiz.why: Entropy and Gini are strictly concave, so they credit partial progress toward purity. The error rate depends only on the majority class and often shows no change.

quiz.q: A numeric feature takes 7 distinct values across 20 training examples. How many candidate thresholds does CART test for it?
quiz.why: Thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct sorted values, and 7 distinct values leave 6 gaps. Splitting between equal values is impossible.

quiz.q: A categorical feature with 6 levels is used in a regression tree. Sorting the levels by mean response reduces the binary partitions CART must test from
wrong: 63 to 6
32 to 6
6 to 5
quiz.why: There are 2⁵ − 1 = 31 binary partitions of 6 levels. Along the sorted order only the 5 cut points need testing, and this is optimal for regression.

quiz.q: A regression leaf contains the targets 4, 6 and 11. What is the sum of squared errors of the leaf around its prediction?
quiz.why: The leaf predicts the mean, 7, so the squared errors are 9, 1 and 16, which sum to 26. Measuring around the median, 6, would give 29.

quiz.q: On what kind of data does stopping at a minimum-gain threshold fail badly?
quiz.a: XOR-like data, where the first split gains almost nothing but enables strong splits below it
wrong: Data whose features are on very different scales, so gains cannot be compared across features
Data with a numeric target instead of classes
Data with more training examples than features
quiz.why: For balanced XOR data no single split reduces impurity, so a gain threshold stops the tree at the root. Post-pruning avoids this by growing first and cutting later.

quiz.q: In a tree, node t as a single leaf has error 0.10, while its subtree has 4 leaves and error 0.04. At what α does collapsing the subtree begin to pay off?
quiz.why: Collapsing removes 4 − 1 = 3 leaves and adds 0.06 error, so it pays once 3α ≥ 0.06, which is α ≥ 0.02. Dividing by 4 forgets that the collapsed node keeps one leaf.

quiz.q: Why is α chosen by cross-validation rather than by minimizing the training error R(T)?
quiz.a: Training error never rises as leaves are added, so it always favors the largest tree
wrong: Cross-validation is cheaper than computing R(T)
R(T) is undefined for pruned trees
A pruned tree has higher training error than a larger tree for every α
quiz.why: The fully grown tree has the lowest training error, so training error alone cannot justify pruning. Held-out error shows when extra leaves only fit noise.

quiz.q: After sorting a feature once, CART can score all thresholds for it in a single pass. Why?
quiz.a: Moving the threshold past one example only shifts that example from the right child to the left, so the class counts update incrementally
wrong: Only the median threshold can ever give the best split
The impurity does not depend on which examples are on each side
The gain increases steadily as the threshold moves right
quiz.why: Each step changes the class counts of the two children by one example, so the impurity is updated in constant time. The cost per node is dominated by sorting.

quiz.q: A tree reports a unique customer ID as its most important feature, though it carries no real signal. Why?
quiz.a: Impurity-based importance favors features with many distinct values, which offer many chances to fit noise
wrong: A unique ID is causally related to every label
Importance is measured on held-out data, so it is reliable
IDs are numeric, and numeric features always outrank categorical ones
quiz.why: A feature with a unique value per row can isolate examples in a tree and reduces impurity on the training set. Permutation importance on held-out data would show no drop.

quiz.q: Why does averaging many trees trained on different samples improve on a single deep tree?
quiz.a: Each deep tree has low bias but high variance, and averaging reduces variance
wrong: Averaging lowers the bias of every individual tree
Averaging makes each tree shallower and easier to read
Averaging removes the need to choose split thresholds
quiz.why: Deep trees fit the training data closely but change a lot with the sample. Averaging cancels part of that variation while leaving the average bias in place.

quiz.q: A regression tree is trained on y = 2x for x between 0 and 10. What does it predict at x = 20?
quiz.a: About 20, the value of its rightmost leaf
wrong: 40, because it learns the line
About 10, the mean of all training targets
Zero, since x = 20 lies outside every leaf
quiz.why: Predictions are piecewise constant, and the rightmost box extends to infinity. The tree cannot extrapolate a trend beyond the training range.

summary: A decision tree partitions the feature space into axis-aligned boxes with a constant prediction in each: the majority class or the mean.
Splits are chosen to reduce impurity: entropy, Gini impurity or (for regression) squared error. Information gain is the parent impurity minus the size-weighted child impurities.
CART grows the tree greedily, testing all features and thresholds at each node.
Control overfitting by stopping rules or by cost-complexity pruning, R(T) + α|T|, with α chosen by cross-validation.
Trees are interpretable, scale-free and flexible but unstable. Ensembles of trees fix the instability.

problems.q: A node has class counts (8, 2). Compute its entropy and Gini impurity.
A parent node has (5+, 5−). A split yields left (4+, 1−) and right (1+, 4−). Compute the Gini gain.
problems.solution: Parent Gini = 0.5. Each child has proportions (0.8, 0.2) so Gini = 0.32. Weighted = 0.5(0.32) + 0.5(0.32) = 0.32. Gain = 0.18.

problems.q: Data (x, y): (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 11). Find the best split threshold for a depth-1 regression tree and the leaf predictions.
problems.solution: Candidates: x ≤ 1.5: SSE_left 0, right mean 8, SSE = 16 + 1 + 9 = 26. x ≤ 2.5: left mean 3, SSE 2; right mean 10, SSE 2; total 4. x ≤ 3.5: left mean 5, SSE 9 + 1 + 16 = 26; right 0; total 26. Best: x ≤ 2.5.
problems.a: Split at x ≤ 2.5, leaf values 3 and 10, total SSE 4.

problems.q: A tree has 12 leaves and training error 0.04. A pruned subtree has 5 leaves and error 0.075. Find the α at which the two trees have equal cost-complexity, and which tree is preferred for α = 0.01.
problems.solution: Equal cost: 0.04 + 12α = 0.075 + 5α, so 7α = 0.035 and α = 0.005. At α = 0.01 the large tree costs 0.04 + 0.12 = 0.16 and the small tree 0.075 + 0.05 = 0.125, so the small tree is preferred.
problems.a: α = 0.005; the 5-leaf tree is preferred at α = 0.01.

problems.q: Why can a tree not represent an arbitrary diagonal boundary x₁ = x₂ with a few splits?
problems.solution: Each split is axis-aligned, so the boundary must be approximated by a staircase. Accuracy of the approximation grows only with the number of splits (about 1/ε steps for resolution ε).
problems.a: Axis-aligned splits approximate a diagonal only by a staircase of many splits.
